title: Testing the booking service
idea: A test case runs one small scenario against your code and checks one expected result, so a change that breaks a rule fails loudly.
points: Each test follows arrange, act, assert: set up state, call once, check.
Test the boundaries: back-to-back slots, reversed times, an exact overlap.
Assert on the stable error `code()`, not on the message text.
Replace listeners with a test double that records what it heard.

code.title: Hand-made test runner
code.caption: JUnit is not available here, so a tiny `check` method plays its role. To stay short, these checks share one service and build on each other; JUnit gives each `@Test` a fresh instance, as the next tab shows.

walk.text: Arrange: a recording test double (a spy), a fresh service and one booking.
The boundary case: a slot starting exactly when the last one ends.
Error cases assert the stable `code()`, never the wording of the message.
The spy proves refused bookings never reach the listeners.
`check` counts and prints; `errorOf` turns a thrown exception into its code.
A test double: a real `BookingListener` that only records ids.

code.title: The same test in JUnit 5
code.caption: JUnit creates a new test object per `@Test`, so `svc` starts empty each time. Mockito could replace the lambda listener with a mock you verify.

pitfalls: Never keep the service in a `static` field; tests then leak bookings into each other.
Test only the happy path and an off-by-one overlap bug ships unnoticed.
Asserting on exception messages breaks tests whenever someone rewords them.

quiz.q: What is the last line `BookingServiceTest` prints?
quiz.why: Four `check` calls run and all hold. `errorOf` catches each `BookingException`, so no exception escapes `main`.

takeaway: One scenario per test, boundaries included, asserted on stable codes.
